Title: Innovative transformer neural network for wind density function estimation at different hub heights of turbine
Text:
Innovative transformer neural 
network for wind density function 
estimation at different hub heights 
of turbine
Amit Kumar Yadav1, Vibha Yadav2 & Walle Tilahun3
Accurate estimation of wind power potential is important for resource assessment to install wind 
turbine. Weibull distribution functions (WDF) have been widely used and it is a function of wind 
speed (WS). With Turbine hub height WS get changes and it form complex nonlinear equations with 
WDF. To compute this paper introduces an innovative Transformer Neural Network (TNN) model for 
WDE estimation leverage self attention mechanism to capture complex pattern. For this wind power 
potential (WPP) of a site located in the Northeastern India is selected. The novelty is that WPP is 
performed up to 80 m height and not up to a 150 m height for North-Eastern India. Cubic Factor (CF) 
method is used for the evaluation of Weibull parameters, i.e., scale ‘c’ and shape ‘k’. CF and k are 
independent of height and are found to be 1.96 and 1.95, respectively. The scale varies from 2.65 to 
3.90 from height 10 m to 150 m. TNN performance is evaluated by Mean Squared Error (MSE), Root 
Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), R-squared (R²), Mean Bias Error (MBE), and 
Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE). For the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF), the model 
achieved an MSE of 0.0012, RMSE of 0.0357, MAE of 0.0238, R² of 0.9170, MBE of -0.0071, and MAPE 
of 12.3158%. In comparison, the Weibull density functions (WDF) estimation yielded an MSE of 0.0003, 
RMSE of 0.0178, MAE of 0.0130, R² of 0.9039, MBE of -0.00018, and MAPE of 11.67%. The results 
demonstrate the Transformer model’s high accuracy and robustness in estimating WDF, making it a 
reliable tool for assessing wind energy potential at different turbine hub heights.
Keywords  Cubic factor, Weibull, Wind power density, Wind potential, Transformer
Wind energy (WE) is one of the renewable energy (RE) sources with the second-fastest growth rates, right after 
solar, and has recently entered a competitive market1,2. A site’s potential for wind power is reflected by its wind 
power density (WPD), which is measured in watts per square meter. WE have highly stochastic drift that can be 
estimated with certain level of accuracy. Wind patterns change, disrupting the grid and affecting stability and 
power quality. This makes it necessary to understand the nature of wind variation at different sites. The wind 
power varies from 0 to 7.2 W/m2 globally. Wind power generation capacity in India has significantly increased in 
recent years. As of 31 March 2025, the total installed wind power capacity reached 50.00 gigawatts (GW)3. By the 
end of 2028, global operational wind capacity is projected to exceed 1,800 GW. Corresponding to this expansion, 
the demand for wind technicians is anticipated to rise beyond 532,4004. According to the global wind energy 
status report for 2025, China maintained its leadership by installing 79.8 GW of new capacity during 2024. The 
United States contributed approximately 4.1 GW, marking a decline attributed to policy uncertainties, while 
Europe collectively added 18.3 GW, with the Netherlands and the UK being major contributors5.
As of April 2025, India ranks as the world’s fourth-largest wind energy producer, with a total installed 
capacity nearing 50 GW. In 2024, the country added around 3.4 GW of new wind capacity, reflecting a 21% 
growth compared to the previous year6. Most of the wind installations are concentrated in the states of Tamil 
Nadu, Gujarat, and Karnataka. According to the National Institute of Wind Energy (NIWE), India’s wind energy 
potential is estimated at 1,163.9 GW at a height of 150 m7. The majority of wind installations are concentrated 
in the southern and western states, notably Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, and Karnataka. To harness wind energy wind 
power potential (WPP) is required for different sites.

Different studies in literature undertaken to assess WPP at different heights are shown in Table 1.
From preceding literature review it is found that most of the WPP studies are performed up to 135 m. No 
study is reported for WPP up to 150 m except for South India29. Therefore, there is a need to perform WPP 
studies at 150 m for other Indian sites. WPP varies with geographical location, atmospheric conditions and 
hub height. Traditional method such as machine learning, empirical models fails to capture temporal and non 
linear patterns in wind with different heights30. Given Transformer Neural Networks success there is necessity to 
develop Innovative Transformer Neural Network (ITNN) specifically tailored to model wind density function at 
various turbine hub heights with higher accuracy.
The first objective is to present an exploratory WPP computation up to 150 m with 10 m increments. The 
second objective is to estimate Weibull distribution functions using innovative Transformer Neural Network.
This work is novel and makes a significant addition because it shows that WPP is only done up to an 
80-meter height and it is not performed up to a 150 m height for North East part of India. Cubic Factor 
(CF) method is used for the evaluation of Weibull parameters (scale ‘c’ and shape ‘k’). Finally, the WDF 
is modeled with novel Transformer Neural Network. This study is organized as follows: Methodology is 
shown in Section II followed by the obtained results and their discussion in Section III. Finally, conclusions 
are given in Section IV.
Methodology
Site selection
The selected site is P Leikul village and is located in Mahur Tehsil of Dima Hasao district in Assam, India. Assam 
is a state in northeastern part of India and it covers 78,438 km2 area. The temperature varies from 43 to 46 °F in 
winter and 5 –38 °C in summer. It experiences heavy rainfall and high humidity.
The total geographical area of P Leikul village is 247.84 hectares and household is 80. The monthly average 
wind speed of selected site P Leikul in Assam India is shown in Fig. 1. The highest wind speed of 4.3 m/s is 
observed in June, lowest of 0.3 m/s in December and average of 2.35 m/s as shown in Fig. 2. These data are taken 
from national aeronautics and Space administration (NASA).

In Assam, Barak and Brahmaputra river has more than fifty tributaries, which causes flood in monsoon 
period every year. The floods cover 39.58% of the total land area and limit power generation capacity 
of Assam. This causes hindrance on overall state economic growth. Moreover, due to power shortage, 
populations in remote areas are not getting sufficient power. Development of renewable energy (RE) based 
generation is of utmost importance in these regions. Among RE resources, WE is very accessible, CUF for 
Assam varies from 0 to 20% and WPP at 120 m is 246 MW. Therefore, it is necessary to do preliminary 
assessment of WPP for different sites at different height for Assam India.

Results and discussion
The Wind Power Potential assessment is calculated using Power law, Weibull model, Cubic Factor (CF) 
method up to the height of 150 m in the difference of 10 m for P Leikul Assam in India. The Wind power 
density (WPD) at height varies from 10 m to 150 m at step of 10 m is shown in Table 2. The wind speed, 
average wind speed, CDF and WDF at height vary from 10 m to 150 m at step of 10 m are shown in Figs. 5, 
6, 7, 8, 9 and 10. The variation of WS, CDF and WDF with heights is shown in Tables 3, 4 and 5.
The average wind speed varies from 2.35 m/s to 3.46 m/s at height variation from 10 m to 150 m showing 
increase in 47.17%. The wind shear coefficient is 0.1429 with height 10 m and 150 m respectively. CF and 
shape parameters are independent of heights and its values are 1.96 and 1.95. This site has fairly windy site. 
The scale parameter varies from 2.65 to 3.90 at height of 10 m to 150 m, which shows increase of 47.17%. 
WPD varies from 15.49 W/m2 to 49.51 W/m2 showing increase of 68.71%. The correlation between wind 
speed and height is developed showing regression value of 99.67%. The average CDF varies from 0.28 to 
0.21 with decrease of 25% and it is constant from 110 m to 150 m. The decrease in WDF from 0.192 to 
0.13 shows decrease of 32.29%.
Prediction of CDF and WDF by transformer model
The correlation heat matrix is shown in Fig. 11. There is a strong positive correlation between WS and CDF. This 
suggests that as the wind speed increases, the CDF value also tends to increase. The high correlation indicates 
a significant linear relationship between these two variables. There is a weak negative correlation between WS 
and WDF. This suggests that there is a slight tendency for the wind speed to decrease as the wind direction 
factor increases, but the relationship is weak and might not be practically significant. There is an extremely weak 
positive correlation between CDF and WDF, almost negligible. This suggests that changes in the wind direction 
factor have almost no linear relationship with the cumulative distribution function values.
MSE measures the average squared difference between the predicted values and the actual values. A lower 
MSE indicates better model performance. The smaller MSE for WDF suggests that the model’s predictions for 
WDF are more accurate compared to CDF. RMSE is the square root of MSE and provides the error in the same 
units as the target variable. A lower RMSE indicates a better fit. The RMSE for WDF is lower, indicating more 
precise predictions compared to CDF. MAE measures the average magnitude of errors in a set of predictions, 
without considering their direction. It is easier to interpret compared to MSE or RMSE. The lower MAE for 
WDF suggests that the model is more accurate in predicting WDF values. R² indicates the proportion of the 
variance in the dependent variable that is predictable from the independent variable. Error matrix is shown in 
Table 6. Both CDF and WDF have high R² values, indicating that the models explain a significant proportion of 
the variance. The slightly higher R² for CDF suggests a marginally better model fit for CDF compared to WDF. 
MBE indicates the average bias in the model’s predictions. Negative values indicate underestimation, while 
positive values indicate overestimation. Both metrics show slight underestimation, with WDF having a very

Conclusions
This study presents an innovative Transformer Neural Network approach for estimating the Wind Density 
Function (WDF) at various turbine hub heights, specifically focusing on Site P in Leikul, Assam, India. The 
analysis reveals that wind speed at the standard 10-meter height is inadequate for effective power generation. 
Consequently, a detailed Wind Power Potential (WPP) assessment was conducted using the Cubic Factor (CF) 
method, Power Law, and the Weibull model across heights ranging from 10 m to 150 m, with 10-meter intervals.
The study highlights that while the CF and shape parameter remain constant across heights, the scale 
parameter increases proportionally with height. Notably, the wind speed and Wind Power Density (WPD) 
exhibit exponential growth with elevation, indicating significant improvement in energy potential at greater 
hub heights. At this site, the mean, maximum, and minimum wind speeds are 2.35 m/s, 4.3 m/s, and 0.3 m/s 
respectively, with a shape parameter (K) of 1.95. The WPD values vary between 15.49 W/m² and 49.51 W/m², 
classifying the region under wind class 1. Wind speed enhancement was observed to rise from 10.28% at 20 m 
to 47.19% at 150 m compared to the base height of 10 m.
The proposed Transformer model demonstrates superior performance for WDF estimation compared to 
the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) model, as evidenced by lower MSE, RMSE, MAE, and MAPE 
values, and high R² values for both models. Minimal mean bias error (MBE) further indicates the reliability and 
accuracy of the predictions.
